prize_parts.citation: for establishing the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered pricing and interest-rate rules, and integrating them into the microfounded framework that underlies modern monetary policy analysis

statement.case_for: The New Keynesian framework is among the most consequential bodies of work in macroeconomics, in both theory and practice. Calvo's time-dependent pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's welfare-based synthesis are three distinct, identifiable building blocks of a framework used daily in central-bank analysis. The ideas date from the 1980s to the 2000s, so they have had decades of testing, extension and criticism. In my opening I ranked B007 first and B014 second. Having read the other members' openings, I now place B014 first. My opening called the attribution in B014 the hardest to defend, and I now think it is more tractable than I said. The ballot's credited list is broad, but the core contributions separate into three conceptually different pieces, each tied to a clear originating body of work. B007 remains scientifically respectable, but the credit there is diffuse and overlaps with other candidacies, as explained below.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Eight names are credited, and any three-person cut leaves out major contributors. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have serious claims, especially for the estimated medium-scale DSGE strand and the New Keynesian Phillips curve and policy analysis. A prize to the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio would honour the conceptual foundations rather than the empirical implementation. A second concern is that the baseline model's empirical adequacy has been questioned after 2008 and again after the post-2020 inflation episode. A third is that earlier macroeconomics prizes already cover nearby ground (rational expectations, DSGE and time-series methods).

responses.point: Krusell ranks B014 first. He sees Calvo's time-dependent pricing and Taylor's staggered contracts and rule as the foundational pieces, with Woodford supplying the welfare-theoretic synthesis. He holds that the post-2021 inflation episode has not undermined the core contributions, and he calls the timing mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I largely agree on the attribution logic, and it is what moved me up from my opening. I would qualify the claim that the inflation episode leaves the core untouched. The framework's qualitative content, price stickiness and policy rules, has survived. The performance of the baseline Phillips-curve specification is more open. That affects how the citation should be worded, which is why mine credits the theory of rigidities and the policy-analysis framework rather than any empirical forecasting performance. I also note that Krusell lists Gali, Gertler and Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans as strong alternatives. I take that as a real cost of the three-person cut, not a footnote.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B014 third with Woodford, Taylor and Gali. He treats the credit as widely spread and says Gertler's 'earlier recognition (2022)' complicates his inclusion. He regards the framework as fully mature, with the post-2021 inflation debate as the main caveat.
responses.response: I would give Gali more weight than my own proposal does, since his work on the New Keynesian Phillips curve and policy analysis is close to the centre of the framework. Where we differ is on Calvo: his pricing device is the specific building block that the rest of the literature depends on, and I would not drop it for Gali. I also think the 2022 point needs correcting. As I understand it, the 2022 prize went to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig, not to Gertler, so Gertler's claim is not weakened by a prior award. The overlap with the 2022 financial-crisis prize bears on B042, not B014. I would still leave Gertler out of this cut, but for reasons of the three-person limit and the separation of strands, not prior recognition.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranks B032 first for its transparent empirical designs and policy influence. She ranks B014 second and flags the post-2008 and post-2021 performance of the New Keynesian framework as its main substantive caveat.
responses.response: I take her caveat seriously and share it. I think the difference between our rankings comes down to what the Committee weights more: the scale and durability of a conceptual framework across decades of policy use, or the credibility of identification in a more recent empirical agenda. B032's China-shock findings remain debated on magnitude and persistence, and the task framework's credit extends beyond the credited names. That is why I keep B032 as an alternative, not as my preferred choice. I do not think the inflation debate is disqualifying. It concerns parameterisation and the Phillips-curve slope more than the underlying logic of nominal rigidity and rules.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B016 first with Persson and Tabellini only, and ranks B014 third with the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio. He regards the B014 cut as defensible but contestable, and asks whether a prize for the framework should split theory from applied-policy contributions.
responses.response: His split between theory and applied-policy contributions is a fair way to frame the question, and I think the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio already covers both. Calvo is theory, Taylor spans contract theory and the policy rule, and Woodford gives the welfare-theoretic policy framework. A split that added the estimation strand would require more names than the configuration allows. On B016, I do not dispute the field's importance. My hesitation is that the 2024 institutions prize covered adjacent ground, and several members flag identification problems in the cross-country constitutional evidence. For B007, Hassler's two-name cut of Saez and Slemrod suggests that even sympathetic members find credit for B007 diffuse, which is part of why I moved off it.

uncertainties: Whether Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum or Smets should displace one of the three proposed names, and whether any three-person award can be defended against the omission of the estimated DSGE strand.
How much the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation debates should weigh against the framework when the award is for conceptual foundations rather than forecasting performance.
Whether the Committee views B014 as too close to earlier macroeconomics prizes on rational expectations, DSGE and time-series methods.

Whether B007 (my opening first choice) should be pursued instead. I moved off it because of its diffuse credit and its overlap with Saez's name in B013 and Chetty's in B021. I have not fully resolved whether the empirical optimal-taxation core could be recognised more narrowly (for example Saez and Slemrod).
Whether the Committee prefers B010 or B032 as an alternative if B014 proves contested. I regard B010 as the cleaner attribution and B032 as the more policy-salient but more debated case.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile with respect to B014 or the other candidates discussed. My documented connections are SSE affiliation with fellow Committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg, and co-authorships in matching and market design. None of these involves a credited candidate here, and I did not rely on any of them.
